title: CVE-2021-22890: TLS 1.3 session ticket proxy host mixup
excerpt:
## Summary:
(I don't think that this can be easily exploitable, but I am submitting it as a security issue for precaution. I am not looking for a bounty.)

Commit [549310e907e82e44c59548351d4c6ac4aaada114](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/549310e907e82e44c59548351d4c6ac4aaada114)  enables session resumption with TLS 1.3. Curl connections maintain two SSL contexts, one for the proxy and one for the destination. However, curl incorrectly stores session tickets issued by an TLS 1.3 HTTPS proxy under the non proxy context.

The issue is that the logic inside `Curl_ssl_addsessionid` that chooses which context to store the tickets under is incorrect under TLS 1.3. 

```
const bool isProxy = CONNECT_PROXY_SSL();
struct ssl_primary_config * const ssl_config = isProxy ?
  &conn->proxy_ssl_config :
  &conn->ssl_config;
const char *hostname = isProxy ? conn->http_proxy.host.name :
  conn->host.name;
```

```
#define CONNECT_PROXY_SSL()\
  (conn->http_proxy.proxytype == CURLPROXY_HTTPS &&\
  !conn->bits.proxy_ssl_connected[sockindex])
```

One of the major differences between how TLS session tickets are issued between TLS 1.3 and prior versions  of TLS is that TLS 1.3 issues session tickets in a *post* handshake message. What this means in practice is that TLS 1.3 tickets are delivered in the first call to `SSL_read()`, rather than being issued as part of `SSL_connect()`. Consequently, `CONNECT_PROXY_SSL()` will see that the proxy has already been connected (since the call to `SSL_connect()` to the proxy was completed), so the call to `Curl_ssl_addsessionid` believes the `isProxy` is `false`, and it stores the ticket under the non proxy context.

After the `CONNECT` call returns successfully, a connection to the original destination will be made through the established TCP tunnel. If the original destination uses https, another TLS handshake will be made. During this TLS handshake, the curl client offers the session ticket of the *proxy* to the destination.

If the proxy is malicious, at this point it could decide to terminate the TLS handshake to the upstream. Since the proxy has the corresponding session ticket key (it was the entity that issued the ticket, after all), it can complete the client -> destination TLS handshake through a resumption. Normally, this would result in a full man in the middle, as TLS certificates are not exchanged as part of a resumed conne

summary: curl incorrectly stores TLS 1.3 session tickets issued by a TLS 1.3 HTTPS proxy under the non-proxy SSL context, leading to potential session ticket misuse during connections to the original destination.

claims.text: curl stores session tickets issued by a TLS 1.3 HTTPS proxy in the wrong SSL context (non-proxy instead of proxy)
claims.reasoning: The function Curl_ssl_addsessionid uses CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() to decide whether to store the session ticket under the proxy SSL context or the destination SSL context. If CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() returns false when a TLS 1.3 ticket arrives (after the proxy handshake completes), the ticket will be stored under the destination context instead of the proxy context.

Selects proxy_ssl_config vs ssl_config based on isProxy

claims.text: The logic in Curl_ssl_addsessionid that selects the SSL context based on CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() is incorrect for TLS 1.3
claims.reasoning: The report quotes a CONNECT_PROXY_SSL definition that checks `!conn->bits.proxy_ssl_connected[sockindex]`. Deterministic checks confirm this definition exists in the codebase. This macro returns false once the proxy SSL connection is marked connected, which happens after SSL_connect() completes. For TLS 1.3, tickets arrive in SSL_read() post-handshake, so the macro incorrectly returns false at ticket storage time.

citations.note: CONNECT_PROXY_SSL defined as FALSE here, but deterministic checks confirm the report's quoted definition exists elsewhere in the codebase

claims.text: When connecting through a TLS 1.3 HTTPS proxy, the first SSL_read() call causes CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() to return false, leading to tickets being stored in the wrong context
claims.reasoning: TLS 1.3 delivers session tickets via NewSessionTicket messages after the handshake (RFC 8446). These arrive in the first SSL_read() call. By that time, the proxy SSL handshake has completed and proxy_ssl_connected is true, so CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() returns false, causing the ticket to be stored under the destination context.

citations.note: isProxy determined by CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() at ticket storage time
RFC 8446 Section 4.6.1: NewSessionTicket sent after client Finished message, i.e., post-handshake

claims.text: The proxy's session ticket can be presented to the original destination, potentially enabling a limited man-in-the-middle if the proxy certificate includes the destination's hostname
claims.reasoning: When the proxy ticket is stored under the destination context, curl will offer it when initiating a new handshake to the destination. The proxy (which issued the ticket) can complete the resumption handshake. Certificate validation in ossl_connect_step3 checks the certificate from the SSL_SESSION used for resumption — which is the proxy's certificate. If that certificate contains the destination hostname, validation passes, enabling a limited MITM.

key_reasons: Curl_ssl_addsessionid uses CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() to select SSL context for ticket storage (lib/vtls/vtls.c:495-500)
CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() returns false after proxy SSL handshake completes (per report's quoted definition, confirmed by deterministic checks)
TLS 1.3 tickets arrive post-handshake in SSL_read() (RFC 8446 Section 4.6.1), when CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() is already false
This causes proxy tickets to be stored under the destination context, so they are offered to the destination on subsequent connections

A malicious proxy can resume the handshake using its ticket; certificate validation uses the proxy cert from the SSL_SESSION, and if it contains the destination hostname, validation passes (ossl_connect_step3 at lib/vtls/openssl.c:3980)
The vulnerability requires a trusted proxy cert that includes the destination hostname — plausible in corporate environments with HTTPS proxies
reply: Thank you for the detailed report and reproducer. The issue is confirmed: Curl_ssl_addsessionid uses CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() to choose the SSL context, but for TLS 1.3 the session ticket arrives in SSL_read() after the proxy handshake completes, so CONNECT_PROXY_SSL() incorrectly returns false. This stores the proxy ticket under the destination context, allowing it to be offered to the destination. A malicious proxy with a cert covering the destination hostname can then MITM the connection. We will fix the context selection logic for TLS 1.3 tickets.
